title: Before You Text Your Ex… Read This First.
paragraphs:
Before You Text Your Ex… Read This First.
The Message You’re About to Send Might Reopen a Door God Has Already Closed—or Become the Beginning of a Redemption Only Christ Can Write.
Your finger hovers over the screen.
You already typed the message.
Maybe it's only two words.
"Hey... how have you been?"
Maybe it's much longer.
You've rewritten it seven times.
Deleted it.
Typed it again.
Read it.
Stared at it.
You tell yourself you're only looking for closure.
Only checking if they're okay.
Only being kind.
Only seeing what happens.
But if you're honest before God...
this message isn't really about your phone.
It's about your heart.
Because sometimes the most dangerous conversations begin long before we ever press "Send."
They begin where no one else can see.
In loneliness.
In regret.
In memories that became idols.
In wounds that never fully healed.
In the quiet moments when the enemy whispers that maybe going backward will finally move you forward.
That whisper has existed since the beginning.
Scripture introduces us to temptation not as something loud, but as something persuasive. The serpent's first words in Genesis were not commands but questions.
In Hebrew, Genesis 3:1 records the serpent asking:

הֲאַף כִּי־אָמַר אֱלֹהִים
"Ha'af ki amar Elohim?"
Literally:
"Did God really say...?"
The strategy has never changed.
Before Satan changes behavior, he attempts to change belief.
Before he attacks obedience, he attacks trust.
Before you question your actions, he teaches you to question God's wisdom.
Maybe that text isn't sinful by itself.
The deeper question is why you want to send it.
Jesus never reduced righteousness to visible actions.
He exposed invisible motives.
When asked about adultery, He reached past behavior into desire.
Matthew 5:28 says in Greek:

πᾶς ὁ βλέπων... πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι
"pas ho blepōn... pros to epithymēsai"
The key word is ἐπιθυμῆσαι (epithymēsai).
It means "to desire," "to long for," "to set one's heart upon."
Jesus teaches that the heart can already travel somewhere the body has not yet gone.
Likewise, a text message may be only a few words, yet the heart may already be rebuilding a bridge God dismantled for your protection.
Sometimes we confuse nostalgia with God's leading.
But nostalgia edits reality.
It remembers the laughter and forgets the manipulation.
It remembers the chemistry and forgets the compromise.
It remembers the affection and forgets the anxiety.
It remembers the beginning but edits out the ending.
The human heart is astonishingly skilled at rewriting history.
Jeremiah warns us plainly:
"The heart is deceitful above all things and desperately sick; who can understand it?" (Jeremiah 17:9).
The Hebrew word for "deceitful" is עָקֹב (ʿaqov).
It carries the idea of being crooked, insidious, or unreliable.
Our emotions are real, but they are not always reliable guides.
That is why Scripture consistently calls believers to submit feelings beneath God's truth rather than allowing feelings to become their authority.
Maybe you think your story is unique.
Maybe it is.
But temptation rarely is.
It simply changes clothes.
Sometimes it wears romance.
Sometimes regret.
Sometimes curiosity.
Sometimes loneliness.
Sometimes it wears the face of someone you once loved.
Paul understood how subtle spiritual battles become.
Ephesians 6:11 tells believers:
"Put on the whole armor of God."
The Greek phrase is:

πανοπλίαν τοῦ Θεοῦ
"panoplian tou Theou"
The full armor.
Not partial armor.
Because partial obedience leaves exposed places.
Many believers faithfully guard what they watch, yet neglect what they reopen emotionally.
Many resist obvious sin while quietly entertaining old attachments.
Many pray for freedom while repeatedly revisiting the chains Christ already broke.
There is a reason Israel was repeatedly commanded not to return to Egypt.
Egypt had become more than a location.
It became a symbol of bondage.
Freedom often feels unfamiliar.
Bondage feels familiar.
Familiarity can masquerade as safety.
Yet God does not call His people back to slavery simply because slavery once felt comfortable.
Maybe your ex has changed.
Maybe they truly have.
People can repent.
Lives can be transformed.
Relationships can be restored.
God is absolutely able to redeem broken people.
But biblical restoration is never built on emotional impulse.
It is built on repentance, truth, wisdom, accountability, and fruit worthy of repentance.
John the Baptist declared:
"Bear fruit in keeping with repentance."
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) means far more than feeling sorry.
It means a transformed mind that results in a transformed life.
Real repentance produces visible fruit.
Not merely convincing words.
Not emotional apologies.
Not temporary excitement.
Changed direction.
Changed character.
Changed priorities.
If those realities are absent, hope may simply be wearing the mask of denial.
And yet there is another possibility.
Perhaps this article is not primarily about your ex.
Perhaps it's about the deeper ache beneath the desire to reach out.
The longing to be chosen.
To be seen.
To be wanted.
To be loved.
Every human heart carries those desires because we were created for communion with God.
When we expect another person to satisfy what only Christ can ultimately fulfill, relationships begin carrying a weight they were never designed to bear.
No boyfriend.
No girlfriend.
No spouse.
No former love.
No future love.
No human being can permanently satisfy a soul created for eternity.
Augustine captured this truth centuries ago when he wrote that our hearts remain restless until they rest in God.
Scripture says it even more beautifully.
Psalm 73:26 declares:
"My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever."
Forever.
Not temporarily.
Not until another relationship appears.
Forever.
Jesus did not come merely to improve broken romances.
He came to redeem broken people.
That is why the Gospel is never simply about getting your old life back.
It is about receiving a brand-new life.
Second Corinthians 5:17 announces:
"If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation."
The Greek says:

καινὴ κτίσις
"kainē ktisis."
Not repaired creation.
New creation.
Christ does not simply patch shattered identities.
He makes people new.
Sometimes that means restoring relationships.
Sometimes it means ending them forever.
Wisdom is learning to treasure the Giver above every gift.
Maybe tonight the Holy Spirit isn't asking you to send a message.
Maybe He's asking you to surrender one.
Delete it.
Not because the other person is beyond God's grace.
But because your obedience belongs to Christ first.
The greatest love story in your life is not the one that ended.
It is the One that refused to end when you deserved judgment.
The Gospel is scandalous because Jesus stepped into our betrayal, carried our shame, bore our sin, and rose again so that failures would never have the final word.
This is why our theme is more than a slogan.
From Scandal to Grace is the story of Scripture itself.
Abraham failed.
David failed.
Peter failed.
Paul persecuted the church.
Yet Jesus rewrote their stories through repentance, grace, and faithful obedience.
He still does.
He can rewrite yours.
Before you press "Send," ask a better question than, "Will this work out?"
Ask, "Will this glorify Christ?"
Ask, "Does this reflect the new creation He has made me to be?"
Ask, "Am I acting from faith, or from fear, loneliness, guilt, nostalgia, or unresolved hurt?"
Those questions may save you from reopening a chapter God has already redeemed.
Be honest before the Lord.
You may never know how God uses a simple act of faithfulness to interrupt a destructive decision and point someone back to Christ.
One surrendered decision today may become the testimony that glorifies Christ for the rest of your life.
